tip: 'Hoppas' always ends in '-s' though its meaning is active: 'jag hoppas att ni alla har det bra'.
'Hit' = to here (movement toward the speaker); 'här' is the static here: 'komma hit'.
'Ta sig tid' = make time; the reflexive 'dig' is required: 'du tog dig tid'.
Pain uses 'ha ont i': 'har haft ont i huvudet' = have had a headache, literally have bad in the head.
Months take 'i': 'i december' = in December, 'i juli' = in July.
'Medveten om' = aware of; this adjective fixes its preposition as 'om': 'medveten om att han måste ändra'.
'Kan' has the infinitive 'kunna', used after another verb: 'för att kunna resa' = to be able to travel.
'Gå i skolan' (in) means be a pupil; 'gå till skolan' (to) is the trip. Here: 'alla går i skolan'.
'Åt' marks who benefits: 'ett rum åt dig' = a room for you.
'Brukar' is a verb meaning to usually do something: 'brukar ringa' = usually call.
'Nere' = down as a location; 'ner' is down as motion: 'nere vid hamnen'.
Adjectives normally add '-t' with ett-words: 'rummet var rent' = the room was clean.
Swedish stacks nouns into one word: 'havregrynsgröt' = 'havregryn' (oat flakes) + linking 's' + 'gröt' (porridge).
In a main clause 'inte' comes after the verb: 'du skämtar väl inte'. In a subordinate clause (after 'att', 'om', 'som') 'inte' moves before the verb.
The verb keeps second place even when another word leads: 'september börjar hösten'.
With 'åka', transport takes no article: 'åker spårvagn' = take the tram, 'åker buss' = take the bus.
Jobs drop the article after 'är': 'hon är läkare', not 'en läkare'.
The '-s' ending makes it passive: 'laddas' = is being charged, from 'ladda' = to charge.
'Varm' adds '-t' with ett-words: 'kaffet är varmt' = the coffee is hot.
'Känna sig' means feel; the reflexive 'mig' matches 'jag': 'känner mig trött'.
'Titta' always takes 'på' for what you watch: 'tittar på TV'.
En-words use 'min': 'min syster', 'min bil'. 'Mitt' is for ett-words.
Weather uses 'det' as a placeholder subject: 'det är kallt' = it is cold.
'Barn' is an ett-word that stays the same in the plural: 'ett barn', 'tre barn'.
'På' marks being at a place like a library: 'på biblioteket'.
'Där borta' = over there. When it leads, the verb stays second: 'där borta ligger affären'.
'Lägger mig' is literally lay myself down, the everyday way to say go to bed.
'Börja' normally links straight to the next verb without 'att': 'börjar jobba' = start working.
Ett-words use 'mitt': 'mitt hus'. En-words use 'min' instead.
Floors use 'på' plus an ordinal like 'tredje' (third): 'på tredje våningen' = on the third floor.
